articles.title: 'I think a part of it was Iran': Trump acknowledges war's impact on midterm election losses
articles.description:
'I think a part of it was Iran': Trump acknowledges war's impact on midterm election losses

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 10:21

        
      
    
      
    
                The prices of goods and petrol have risen in the US as a direct result of the unpopular war in Iran, and played a role in the Democrats gaining control of the Senate and House of Representatives
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US President Donald Trump speaks during a round table at the White House in Washington, DC, US, 21 October 2026 (Kevin Lamarque/ Reuters)
                  Off
                  US President Donald Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the war on Iran played a part in the Republican party’s sweeping midterm election losses. 

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, with politicians who had campaigned on their opposition to the war scoring notable victories.

In separate interviews reflecting on the reasons behind his party’s heavy defeats, Trump said: “I think a part of it was Iran… Iran was a piece of it.”

Nevertheless, the US president stood by his decision to join Israel in attacking Iran, which also went against the “no new wars” messaging of his 2024 presidential campaign.

“I did the right thing,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal. “I would have done it again.”
  
    



  



The US and Israel went to war with Iran at the end of February, after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly presented Trump with intelligence from Mossad convincing him that doing so would lead the Iranian people to rise up and overthrow their government. 

Cost of living

But despite killing a slew of Iranian leaders, including former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, the government in Tehran has remained intact and the Iranian military has seized control of the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices skyrocketing across the globe.  

The attendant rise in the cost of petrol and other goods at home in the US was a theme of the Democrats’ messaging, with candidates across the country blaming the war for the high cost of living.

Trump has chopped and changed his stated priorities for the war, which has remained consistently unpopular with Americans. 

Asked after the midterm results about reports that he was considering using a nuclear weapon on Iran, Trump said: “I don’t need it, we’ve knocked them out already, 90 percent.”

In Tehran, the US election results were met with satisfaction. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Wednesday on X.

articles.title: Trump admits Iran war caused election losses but ‘we had to do it’
articles.description:
Trump admits Iran war caused election losses but ‘we had to do it’

    
    

        
    
                US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the Iran war was responsible for his Republican Party's resounding midterm election defeat.

Asked whether he agreed with Vice President JD Vance earlier remarks that the Iran war was "the reason we lost", Trump told reporters outside the White House ballroom construction site that his comments were "largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term".

"But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he added.

He also ruled out firing Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying "he's doing a very good job," despite his role in pushing for military action against Tehran.

articles.title: 'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
articles.description:
'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?

    
    

        
    
                The Democrats secured a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday, but one critical question remains unresolved: is US President Donald Trump now more or less likely to resume the war on Iran with the election cycle over?

Before the midterms, the US appeared to be on the verge of launching a new, wide-scale attack against Iran.

The families of US diplomats were evacuated from the region, and additional US military assets flooded into the Middle East. Arab leaders issued cryptic warnings about a devastating new conflict.

But the attack many diplomats and analysts expected around election day never materialised. In fact, Republicans are now blaming the Iran war, and even Israel, for their blistering defeat at the hands of the Democrats.

Trump said on Wednesday that "it's largely true" the Iran war and high fuel prices tied to the conflict led to his party’s historic defeat.

Read more: 'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?



During a rally in Tehran's Enqelab Square, Iranians stand beneath an anti-US billboard depicting US President Donald Trump, on 4 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)

articles.description:
'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Sean Mathews
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 21:14

        
      
    
      
    
                A collapse in oil prices on Wednesday suggests chances of escalation are dwindling, but some analysts say a bitter Trump might lash out at Tehran
                      
                  
                  

  


                  During a rally in Tehran's Enqelab Square, Iranians stand beneath an anti-US billboard depicting US President Donald Trump, on 4 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
                  Off
                  The Democrats secured a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday, but one critical question remains unresolved: is US President Donald Trump now more or less likely to resume the war on Iran with the election cycle over?

Before the midterms, the US appeared to be on the verge of launching a new, wide-scale attack against Iran.

The families of US diplomats were evacuated from the region, and additional US military assets flooded into the Middle East. Arab leaders issued cryptic warnings about a devastating new conflict.

But the attack many diplomats and analysts expected around election day never materialised. In fact, Republicans are now blaming the Iran war, and even Israel, for their blistering defeat at the hands of the Democrats.

Trump said on Wednesday that "it's largely true" the Iran war and high fuel prices tied to the conflict led to his party’s historic defeat.
  
    



  



"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vice President JD Vance said more bluntly on Wednesday, also blaming the Trump administration’s ties to Israel for his party’s thrashing.

Notably, the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, posted his support for Vance’s analysis on X. People familiar with the White House have described him as an ardent anti-interventionist who has opposed the US war on Iran.

'We are going to end this war'

A nine percent collapse in oil prices on Wednesday reflects a shift in expectations. Merissa Khurma, founder and CEO of Amena Strategies, told Middle East Eye that an election outcome could see Trump’s inner circle and Congress constrain the president from resuming the war.

“This all depends on how elected members in the House and Senate work together to ensure a change of course with Iran and what Trump is told by his advisors,” Khurma, who is also a non-resident fellow at the Baker Institute at Rice University, told MEE.


  

  US midterm elections 2026: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to Senate
    Read More »


Several reasons could dismiss this reasoning when it comes to Trump. 

The president has boasted about his “veto power” over Congress.

While Trump told Politico on Tuesday during election coverage that he didn't want to just "sit around there for two years vetoing everything", the 80-year-old billionaire who is prohibited from running for a third term may also feel unconstrained by lawmakers.

Under the Constitution, only Congress has the authority to declare war, but the last US president who sought out congressional approval for the use of military force was George W Bush in 2001 and 2002.

Still, experts say the scale of the Democrats' victory could constrain Trump. With 54 seats in the US Senate and 237 in the House, the party has a comfortable cushion that will give it subpoena and investigative power.

“It is hard to predict what Trump will do, but it matters how Democrats work with Republicans willing to cooperate on stopping further escalation,” Khurma said.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer put the Iran war at the heart of the Democratic Party’s agenda on Wednesday.

“We are going to end the war,” Schumer said.

"We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he added.
  
    



  



Despite this rhetoric and downward move in oil prices, the deployment of military assets in the Middle East suggests escalation is likely.

'Trump is freed up'

The US has two aircraft carrier groups and an amphibious assault ship in the Arabian Sea. A third aircraft carrier group is arriving in the region.


  

  Houthis launched cross border raids on Saudi military posts, sources say
    Read More »


Meanwhile, Iran’s leadership appeared to savour Trump’s political collapse.

“The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz - and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington,” Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X.

Even as Trump acknowledged the Iran war played a part in his party’s stunning defeat, he expressed no doubts about launching a war on Iran at the start of the year.

"I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” he said.

Some experts say that a bitter US president with no electoral constraints may decide to resume attacking Iran.

“If anything, Trump is now freed up for another round of strikes,” Alan Eyre, a former senior State Department expert on Iran, now at the Middle East Institute, told MEE.

“The new Congress won’t be seated until January, and even then it is questionable how much real ability they will have to constrain the president, so I don’t think it changes much,” he said.

articles.title: The Trump era is over. The world should take note
articles.description:
The Trump era is over. The world should take note

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
David Hearst
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 21:38

        
      
    
      
    
                If the Netanyahu camp is trembling at where the US appears to be headed, Gulf leaders should be in no less than a panic
                      
                  
                  

  


                  An Iranian demonstrator carries a placard depicting US President Donald Trump during a rally in Tehran, on 4 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
                  Off
                  It took nine months, but regime change has finally been achieved. 

Nine months after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad director David Barnea put the idea into US President Donald Trump’s head that regime change was possible, it has been achieved. 

The only variation on the plan that all three men worked on is that regime change has happened in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, Georgia, Florida, and in Congress - not in Tehran. 

The war on Iran is the defining mistake of Trump’s second term as president, and of Netanyahu’s final term of office - but Iran is by no means their sole nemesis. 

For the president who knew nothing about Iran, it was more than a bet that went sour. The fact that it was all Netanyahu’s idea makes failure even worse for the leader of an “America First” movement. Iran is a quintessentially “foreign war” that proved the principle on which Trump himself campaigned. 
  
    



  



Failure in Iran was different for the prime minister who had the Islamic Republic in his sights for most of his adult life.

It was a classic example of military and intelligence overreach. Netanyahu and Mossad thought they could do to a whole country what they thought they had done to two movements: Hamas and Hezbollah. They totally underestimated the power of the Islamic Republic to resist. 

But war on Iran, and the economic disaster it unleashed on both sides of the Gulf and beyond - including record prices at gas stations - are not the real cause of the earthquake that has shaken US politics. 

Common nemesis

The Democrats had to collapse first to let Trump in for a second term. 

They did this by allowing former President Joe Biden to run for a second term, and compounded that error by choosing his vice president, Kamala Harris, to run instead after he dropped out.

Had Harris won that contest in 2024, no Democrat of any stripe would now be talking about ending military aid to Israel.

Biden and Harris had overseen, supported and armed the first and bloodiest days of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, a policy from which they will never recover.


Sayed is the future, and Pelosi is history. That is the measure of political change that Gaza has produced


Gaza was the Democratic Party’s nemesis, just as it was the British Labour Party’s under Keir Starmer. 

It is Gaza that has turned the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) from a force no aspiring US politician would dare to confront into a toxin. It is Gaza that has now become the nemesis of the Republican Party, and the Trump clan, too.

A genocide that was being documented in real time, with images of war crimes often filmed by the perpetrators of these outrages, became the defining issue of the era. 

These images defied any words invented to cover up what was happening. The images were in total contradiction to the US line that Israel was “defending itself”. They electrified the Democratic base, as they did to the millions of progressives worldwide who took to the streets in protest.

Just consider how one of Tuesday night’s spectacular winners, US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, started his political journey.

Sayed began as the classic Christmas tree, upon which anyone could pin anything. He was decried by Trump and by his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, as a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood. 
  
    



  



Trump said “he is a Muslim Brotherhood guy, 100 percent” - and most of the US media reported that false claim faithfully. 

Policy referendum 

Just last week, House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi appeared on a podcast, whose host Donny Deutsch claimed Sayed had made “concerning” comments about the existence of a Jewish state: “That’s antisemitic as far as I’m concerned,” he said.

Pelosi replied: “No, it’s more than concerning. It’s wrong. It’s wrong, and it isn’t a reflection of the Democrats in the Congress of the United States. 

“This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress,” she added threateningly.


  

  Americans voted against war. The Democrats must not mistake that for a mandate
    Read More »


Aipac spent $30m trying to defeat Sayed in the primaries and another $9m supporting the pro-Israel candidate, Rogers, in the midterms. Representative Haley Stevens, defeated by Sayed in the primaries, switched sides spectacularly days before the election, jumping to the Republican camp. 

That alone boosted Sayed’s chances in a tight race, because Stevens was condemned by the very people who had been warned off endorsing Sayed at the start of his campaign.

Well, “this new person” has not only become a reflection of the new Congress. His election in Michigan became the biggest referendum on US policy on Israel that has ever been seen. 

Sayed is the future, and Pelosi is history. That is the measure of political change that Gaza has produced.

The Jerusalem Post was correct to conclude that the election in Michigan alone had grave implications for US support for Israel as a whole.

“One of the clearest takeaways from the election campaign is the political price the war with Iran has exacted on the Republican Party,” its analysis said, referring to the war Israel pushed the US into on 28 February.

“The expansion of the camp critical of Israel, and its growing access to positions of influence, represents a shift that Israel cannot afford to ignore,” it added.

Democratic limits

Of course, we are far from a post-Zionist Democratic Party, still less a Congress that will vote to cut military aid to Israel.

For now, the limits of policy that can be expected from the new crew in Congress have been sketched out by Ro Khanna, the US congressman whose van was surrounded by armed settlers during his last visit to the occupied West Bank.
  
    



  



Khanna has pushed for official US recognition of a Palestinian state, opposed unconditional military aid, and advocated a permanent ceasefire and non-violent resistance - but for all that, he backs Zionism and Israel’s “right to exist”.

“I believe that Zionism is self-determination of the Jewish people, and the right for Israel to exist. And I support that. What I don’t believe is if it means Greater Israel,” Khanna said last year, adding that he believes there must be a “two-state solution”.



In other words, neither Khanna nor anyone else in the “new” Democratic Party is going to do anything about ending apartheid, let alone the occupation. 

In giving credence to the idea that the two-state solution is still possible, Khanna’s position flies in the face of what happened to him during his visit, as well as the unanimous opinion of all Jewish Israeli parties - both pro- and anti-Netanyahu - in last week’s election, all of whom have doomed a Palestinian state.

But here, we should distinguish between the politicians and the movement that propelled them to power. Who would have thought three years ago that US public opinion would have travelled this far? This is a long conflict, and its solution will be long, too. 

The ball is still rolling, and it will not stop.

This global movement supporting Palestinian self-determination will not be assuaged if all that happens is a return to the status quo that reigned on 6 October 2023; if, say, more food and supplies get into Gaza, but the siege itself is maintained, or if settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank calm down, but the settlements themselves remain.

Shaky ground

Across its history, Israel has relied as much on the liberal Zionist support of the centre-left as it has on the neoliberal right. Both those terrains are now shaky ground.

For US Republicans, the lessons of this defeat are even starker. The massive Democratic congressional victory on Tuesday was triggered by soaring living costs, tariffs, and huge instability in US-driven wars.

But behind much of this instability was Trump’s relationship with his two closest allies: Russian President Vladimir Putin and Netanyahu.


However much Trump now tries to claim his name was not on the ballot, the record shows he campaigned in 30 rallies for losers. That is not a good look for a populist


The MAGA faithful who have parted company with Trump, like talk show host Tucker Carlson - and even those who have not declared their hand, like Carlson’s friend, Vice President JD Vance - will feel empowered by this result.

Trump will continue to blag that what the US does at home and abroad is what he, the president, and he alone decides to do. The only voice that matters to him is the one in his head. 

He will cast his veto. He will encourage another government shutdown. 

But history has shown there are forces that Trump fears. He fears the bond market and the opinion of Wall Street. He fears the battle for succession.

The time is long past when he could claim to be a victim of the Democratic establishment. He is now one of Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s patriarchs whose autumn might have already come.

However much Trump now tries to claim his name was not on the ballot, the record shows he campaigned in 30 rallies for losers. That is not a good look for a populist.

Tighter scrutiny

Beyond Washington, the midterms will clearly be seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term as president, whether or not Trump limps on as a lame duck.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he expected Washington to continue the war, seeking Tehran’s “unconditional surrender”. 

Perhaps, but a resumption of air strikes would be politically even more suicidal after such a result than it was before. Vance called the result a direct consequence of the Iran war.

Trump is a falling object. As such, everyone but his closest coterie will be less than eager to pick up the phone next time it rings.


  

  'Freed up or congressionally constrained': Is Trump more or less likely to resume war on Iran?
    Read More »


The Trump clan will now come under ever-tighter financial scrutiny from the new Congress. Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chair of the House Oversight Committee, was not joking when he warned Trump to “lawyer up”.

Trump clan members have gorged themselves at the trough of every crisis, every impending tariff. In any other environment, it would be called insider trading. In Trump’s White House, it was business as usual.

All the dealings of his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, will come under ferocious scrutiny.

Of particular interest to the House Oversight Committee will be the Trump family’s lucrative business relationships with foreign investors and government-linked figures, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.

In January 2025, four days before Trump’s inauguration, UAE-backed investors paid $500m for a 49 percent stake in World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded by Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump.

The investment was backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE’s national security adviser and brother of the country’s president.

The Wall Street Journal reported that $187m of the initial payment went to companies linked to the Trump family, while $31m went to companies associated with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s Middle East envoy and a co-founder of the venture.

Clear warning

Following the money, investigators could move seamlessly to all of the Gulf states’ bribes to Trump and his family. 

That probe should include the Board of Peace, which should now, by rights, be scrapped and replaced by a UN international structure.

If the Netanyahu camp in Israel is trembling at where the US appears to be headed, Gulf leaders should be in no less than a panic. 

Iran’s drones and missiles punctured the bubble of security that gave small but intensely wealthy states the illusion that they were protected from the chaos around them.

The midterm results will have a similar effect. They have surely reinforced the message that the Gulf states have been throwing their money away by investing in Trump. 


The internationally powered movement for Palestine that propelled these changes in the US is not going to go away. If anything, it will gather in intensity


True, we do not know what Trump would have done, had they refused to invest in him. Would he have pulled the plug on the vulnerable Turkish economy if President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had not invested so much political capital in Trump? We may never know.

But that time is past. 

For their own security, Middle Eastern powers must turn to regional alliances and mutual defence guarantees as their template for the future.

UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman both built their country’s strategies around Trump. That surely is the worst investment decision either could have made. 

Everyone kowtowed to Trump. Before the main attack on Iran, the Doha Forum in Qatar last year turned itself into a Trump edition. His sons were the stars of the show, and the halls were filled with American delegates. It showed crudely in which direction Qatar was turning.

Europe was no different. Will it now stand up to Trump and turn itself into a real competitor to US policy, especially over Ukraine?

And finally, the midterms contain a very clear warning to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government. 

The internationally powered movement for Palestine that propelled these changes in the US is not going to go away. If anything, it will gather in intensity. 

If Burnham is perceived to be delivering empty promises to Palestinians in particular and the Arab world in general, as former US president Barack Obama did in his Cairo speech, Burnham will suffer the same fate as Starmer.

Talking the talk on Israel’s occupation will not be enough. Burnham will have to walk the walk, too.

articles.title: Trump's midterm defeat gives the Gulf a chance to escape America's forever wars
articles.description:
Trump's midterm defeat gives the Gulf a chance to escape America's forever wars

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Andreas Krieg
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 16:07

        
      
    
      
    
                Regional leaders must use their influence in Congress to prevent another attack on Iran and negotiate a non-aggression pact with Tehran on their own terms
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance in the Oval Office on 16 March 2026. Vance said on 4 November that the war on Iran was 'the reason we lost' the midterms (Annabelle Gordon/AFP/File photo)
                  Off
                  The US midterm elections were fought over the cost of living, the pundits will say. Look closer and a foreign policy verdict comes into view. Voters passed judgment on Washington's role in the Middle East: on its unconditional backing of Israel, and on Donald Trump's war on Iran. Both lost.

Republicans surrendered both houses of Congress, and several states that had voted red for decades turned blue. Commentators have already noted the irony. Trump set out to change the regime in Tehran. Tehran, by outlasting him, helped change the political order in Washington.

The results also mark a turning point for the Israel lobby and its neoconservative hyperactivism. An endorsement from Aipac, the pro-Israel lobby group, once a prized asset, has become a stain that candidates hurry to wash off. The lobby adapted by moving its money through less visible channels.

It spent millions against candidates who questioned America's unequivocal and open-ended military and financial support for an Israeli government that has thrown the region under the bus. In key races, the money failed to move voters.

Michigan offers the clearest case. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who won the state's Senate seat, ran on American interests. His opponents tried to turn the race into a referendum on Israeli ones.
  
    



  



Voters saw through it and punished a Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, whose campaign offered empty pledges of loyalty to Israel and little on the everyday concerns of Michiganders. Washington's loyalty to Israel dragged the US into its worst military defeat since Vietnam.

Unlike the defeats in Iraq or Afghanistan, this one was felt by ordinary Americans at home, in their pockets. The war on Iran left Americans poorer, their country more vulnerable and Washington more exposed in its competition with China and Russia.

Tehran, for its part, played a patient game. It absorbed months of bellicose rhetoric from Israel and the Trump administration, both apparently eager to engineer another round of major war before the vote.

It also refused to hand Trump a diplomatic breakthrough he could campaign on. That calculation carries a risk, as Iran now faces a president who may want to settle scores.

The rise of the Gulf lobby

As the Israel lobby weakens, the Gulf lobby arguably grows stronger. While Israel is a net consumer of American power in the region, the Gulf states have presented themselves as net contributors. They give the US strategic depth in one of the regions most vital to American interests.

They have pledged trillions of dollars of investment in the American economy, and their sovereign wealth funds help underwrite American growth. Qatar and Oman have also repeatedly handed Trump diplomatic off-ramps from quagmires of Israel's making, from Gaza to Iran.

The Gulf states nonetheless remain the most exposed party in the standoff between the US, Israel and Iran. Together with Iran, they have taken the heaviest economic hit and carried most of the war's burden.


What they got was one more pro-Israel president, played with ease by Benjamin Netanyahu in pursuit of the Israeli prime minister's personal agenda


Disillusionment with Trump and the Maga movement in Gulf capitals is palpable. Trump promised to end America's forever wars in the region. Gulf leaders embraced his pledge to make America great again.

What they got was one more pro-Israel president, played with ease by Benjamin Netanyahu in pursuit of the Israeli prime minister's personal agenda.

Riyadh, Doha and Abu Dhabi have therefore begun to imagine a post-American Middle East. In that order, the US keeps a footprint in the region, while its partnership with the Gulf sits inside a wider web of complementary multilateral agreements.

The midterms also let Gulf leaders picture a post-Trump America: more predictable, less erratic and content to stand on the sidelines. That last quality matters most. For the Gulf, an America that stays out of the region's conflicts is now preferable to one that keeps getting sucked into unwinnable adventures and leaves the region worse off each time.

Lame-duck Trump

The Gulf states have already moved toward strategic autonomy and self-reliance. A lame-duck Trump will speed that process. Gulf governments will loosen their overreliance on Washington and supplement the relationship with other partners, Europe among them.

The lasting answer lies in the region itself. The Gulf states and Iran need deeper integration, anchored in a non-aggression pact they negotiate among themselves, with the US outside the room.
  
    



  



Two conditions must hold for this to work. First, the Gulf states have to pool their influence in Washington and spend it on a single goal: preventing an American return to war.


  

  US elections: Races to watch in the 2026 midterms
    Read More »


Another round would hit the Gulf harder than the last, and Israel alone would gain from it. Every military option Trump has floated ends in catastrophe for the Gulf, destroying wealth and leaving the world economy weaker.

Second, someone must build a diplomatic framework acceptable to two sides whose trust in each other is close to zero. Once again, that lonely weight falls on Qatar's shoulders.

Time is short. Trump has little left to lose, and he never cared much for the Republican Party anyway. Without a breakthrough soon, a strike to satisfy his ego becomes more likely, and sooner.

There is one reason for hope. Iran withheld concessions while they would have handed Trump an electoral win. With the votes counted, that motive is gone. Tehran may now prove more flexible, and an interim deal could still get across the line.

American voters have shifted the balance in Washington. Many of the newly elected lawmakers echo the original promise of Maga: an America that leads from behind and works through partners able to take responsibility for their own backyard.

The Gulf lobby must adjust accordingly. Its task now is to court this new generation in Congress, which is challenging the neoconservative dinosaurs of a bygone era and supports the Gulf's readiness to take regional security into its own hands.

articles.title: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
articles.description:
Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Abdallah al-Naami
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 13:47

        
      
    
      
    
                From children playing out to families queuing for food, indiscriminate Israeli shooting has made daily life a struggle for survival across Gaza
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Safia Abo Amra hold a photo of her granddaughter Fatima al-Bayouk, who was killed by Israeli gunfire earlier this month (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
                  Off
                  After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.

Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.

The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.

For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life.

“Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. I have seven sons and six daughters, yet Fatima was more precious to me than all of them,” Abo Amra told Middle East Eye.
  
    



  



Despite everything she had endured, Bayouk had brought joy back into her grandmother’s life. Her uncle Ahmad Abo Amra remembered her as a bright, cheerful girl whose smile lifted the spirits of those around her.


'My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her'

- Safia Abo Amra, Palestinian grandmother 


“The best thing about Fatima was her smile that always brought joy to everyone around her. She was smart, responsible and loved happy occasions like weddings and family gatherings,” he said.

Her death reflects a wider pattern of indiscriminate Israeli gunfire that has become a daily threat to Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, particularly displaced families living near the so-called Yellow Line.

Israeli shooting from military positions, tanks and quadcopter drones has killed and wounded hundreds of civilians since the October 2025 ceasefire. It has also disrupted access to basic necessities and made everyday activities dangerous.

As Israel expands its control over more of the territory, families increasingly find themselves exposed to gunfire, with little protection and few places to seek safety.

A life cut short

For Bayouk’s family, her death was particularly devastating. She had already survived the loss of her immediate family in the early days of Israel’s genocide.

On 13 December 2023, an Israeli air strike targeted their home in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, killing her family. Bayouk survived and went to live with her grandmother in Deir al-Balah, where Abo Amra and other relatives tried to rebuild her life amid the devastation of the war.


'With her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren'

- Safia  Abo Amro


“We did our best to provide everything Fatima needed and make her feel cared for and surrounded by people who love her,” Abo Amra said.

“I wanted to make up for the loss of her family, but with her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren.”

Education remained an important part of Bayouk’s life as she grew up in her grandmother’s home. Concerned for her safety, Abo Amra refused to send her to a UN school after hearing that Israeli stray bullets frequently reached the area. Instead, she paid monthly fees to enrol her in a local school.

“I walked Fatima to school every day. She was very smart and always did her homework before playing,” Abo Amra said.

Her death reopened the grandmother’s wounds.

“I was shocked and couldn't speak or move. Her death was twice as painful for me; it reminded me of my daughter and grandchildren who were killed at the beginning of the war,” Abo Amra said. 

“My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her.”

  
  
      



    Fatima al-Bayouk liked to dress well, her family says (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
  









Despite her young age, Bayouk left a lasting impression on those around her. She loved dressing up, particularly for family celebrations.

Her uncle Reda Abo Amra remembered how much she enjoyed choosing new clothes. The family had recently bought her winter clothes, but she never got the chance to wear them.

“She always liked to be well-dressed. We bought her new clothes for winter, but she was killed before she could wear them,” he told MEE.
  
    



  



Bayouk was not the first member of her family to be killed by Israeli gunfire. Six months before her death, her uncle Masoud Abo Amra, who was born with a mental disability, was shot in the neck while visiting his sister in Khan Younis.

“Masoud was Fatima's favourite uncle. She was devastated when she bid him farewell,” Ahmad said.

‘When the shooting starts, life stops’

For displaced families in Gaza, Israeli gunfire is not only a deadly threat but also a constant disruption to daily life.

Zaid al-Kafarna, 19, and his family of 10 were displaced from northern Gaza to the Um Duhair area, south of Deir al-Balah, days before the October 2025 ceasefire came into effect.

Kafarna said Israeli shooting was initially “occasional” and took place some distance from their tents. But it gradually became more frequent and moved closer to the camp. Over the past three months, he said, it had become a daily threat, frequently causing deaths, injuries and damage. 


  

  Gaza family mourns boys killed by Israel along Yellow Line
    Read More »


“I miraculously survived stray bullets several times. My friend and neighbour, Mohammad Aqel, was killed a few weeks ago by a stray bullet while he was preparing to return to northern Gaza,” Kafarna told MEE.

His mother, Shereen al-Kafarna, was recently wounded by an Israeli bullet while inside their tent. She described how the shooting brings life in the camp to a standstill.

“When the shooting starts, life stops in our camp. Neighbours warn each other. We leave everything and hold the children, then lie on the ground to avoid the bullets hitting around us. Everyone is terrified, especially the children,” she said.

The gunfire also disrupts Palestinians' efforts to secure basic necessities, including food and water.

“Sometimes while we are waiting in queues for water and food, Israeli tanks and quadcopter drones start shooting directly towards us,” Zaid said.

“Everyone panics. We lie on the ground at the side of the road, watching the aid trucks carrying our food and water drive away to escape the bullets. On those days, we don't have anything to eat or drink.” 

Nowhere to go

The pattern of daily Israeli shootings near the Yellow Line, alongside the ongoing expansion of Israel’s buffer zone in Gaza, raised questions among families about whether the gunfire is as random as it appears.

Many believe that the shootings appear to form part of a military tactic to force Palestinian families out of their homes and tents, allowing Israel to expand its control over more territory through force.
  
    



  



In the year following the ceasefire, Israeli control over Gaza grew from 53 to 70 percent, reflecting what the Palestinians describe as a systematic policy of territorial expansion.

Families living near the Yellow Line said the threat of stray bullets had forced several others to leave their camps.

“Watching families leave our camp every day makes us feel even more afraid. We wish we could move away from the bullets, but we have nowhere to go,” Shereen told MEE. 

“Even if we had somewhere to go, we can't afford the extremely expensive cost of transportation.”

With few options for escape, some families have resorted to building small sand barriers and digging trench-like holes inside and between their tents to shelter from the bullets.

  
  
      



    Shadi Siam dug a trench for his family next to their tent to take cover from Israeli gunfire (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
  











Next to his tent, Shadi Siam dug a small trench to protect his family of five.

“I fear for my children's lives every time I hear Israeli stray bullets flying low,” Siam told MEE.

“My children wake up terrified, and I carry them to the hole where we all hide for two to five hours until the shooting stops,” he added.

“I don't know how I will protect them when the winter comes, and the hole becomes unusable.”

articles.title: ‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma
articles.description:
‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE correspondent
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 09:10

        
      
    
      
    
                Renewed fighting around Taiz has left children with nightmares, bedwetting and constant fear, while schools remain closed and psychological support is scarce
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A woman sits with two children in a classroom converted into a temporary shelter for displaced people at Sawkani school, north of Aden, Yemen, 15 September 2026 (AFP)
                  Off
                  In October, as clashes reached Taghreed Abdulellah’s area, located about 30km from Yemen's Taiz city, the mother of three found herself unable to flee with her children, as battles had already broken out in their village.

She had no choice but to gather her children, aged four, seven and 10, in the hallway to protect them from potential blasts or shrapnel coming through the windows.

“Their father wasn’t at home; it was just them and me. The clashes were outside, and an explosion went off right near our home, leaving the children terrified and crying for hours,” Abdulellah told Middle East Eye. 

“I couldn’t stop them from crying; in fact, I broke down and joined them at times.”

When the fighting quieted down, the children would stop crying, and some neighbours visited to boost their morale.
  
    



  



However, as soon as the battles flared up again, the crying resumed.

“This continued for four days until the fierce battles moved away from our area. But my children’s lives have completely changed for the worse,” she explained.

“My children are always angry, and the two younger ones are now suffering from bedwetting, while the eldest constantly talks about losing his life and believes he will be killed at any moment, rather than thinking about his studies and future as he used to.” 

Abdulellah’s children used to sleep in their own room, but since the fighting started, they do not dare to sleep alone. The whole family now sleeps in one room, with the two younger children sleeping in their mother’s arms.

“Nightmares terrify them every night, and during the day they refuse to leave the house because they feel they will be killed or injured if they go outside. So, they spend the entire day indoors,” Abdulellah said.

Battles in Taiz    

Public schools across Taiz governorate, including Taiz city and rural areas, have been closed since 4 October, as it is unsafe for children to attend school.

It is also unsafe for children to play outside, as shelling and air strikes hit almost every district in the area. 
  
    



  



Abdulellah believes it is unsafe for her children to go outside, yet she wants them to be able to so they can resume a normal life and heal from the psychological trauma they are facing.


  

  Yemen war: Taiz villagers face tough choices as fighters move in
    Read More »


“It is the first time in my life that I have seen my children feel so lost. They don’t want to play, they don’t want to study, and they only talk about the war. I am worried this will impact the rest of their lives even when normal life returns.”

On 4 October, Houthi forces advanced into large areas of Taiz governorate, taking control of most of the governorate and seizing all roads leading to Taiz city.

Battles are currently ongoing around Taiz city and in rural areas, as the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, attempt to push from Taiz toward Lahij governorate while also trying to take full control of Taiz city.

Saudi-led air strikes have targeted Houthi forces in the rural areas of Taiz and around Taiz city, which have also taken a heavy toll on children in those areas.

The World Health Organization has reported that 1,677 people were killed and more than 7,395 injured across Yemen between August and late October 2026 amid renewed clashes between government forces and Houthis.

The executive manager of the Taiz Human Rights Centre civil society organization, Mazen Aqlan, told MEE that 19 children were killed and 49 injured in Taiz governorate in October 2026. 

Severe psychological impact   

Odai, 13, is a child in Taiz city whose life has also completely changed. He used to spend his mornings at school and his afternoons playing with friends. But since 4 October, he has spent most of his days and nights scrolling through his phone, only leaving the house briefly to sit with friends and adults under a nearby tree.

The main issue, however, lies in the photos and videos he views on his mobile, along with the stories he hears from adults about what happened in 2015 when fighting reached their neighbourhood and civilians, including children, were killed or injured. 

“Life isn’t easy, and death is close to everyone,” Odai told MEE. “We were focused on our studies and weren’t aware that a person could lose their life in a single minute. That is what happened to many people, both nowadays and during the last war.”


  

  'If Houthi shelling does not kill us, the diseases will': Yemenis in besieged Taiz bemoan neglect
    Read More »


Odai, who is in the seventh grade, appears mature for his age, but the ongoing developments and the stories he hears have shifted his priorities from his education to thoughts of the afterlife, something that is not typical for a child his age.

When asked about his priorities and whether they should focus on his studies, he laughed and said: “Studying is important, but there is no guarantee we will stay alive until schools reopen. Death is closer to us than resuming our education.”

MEE spoke with Odai’s father, in his 50s, who preferred to remain anonymous. He confirmed that Odai was not like this until last month, when he heard a story about a child killed in the city and saw related photos and videos, leaving him deeply affected.

“We do our best to keep our children away from the fighting. We keep them at home and don’t allow them to venture outside, especially to far areas, but it is difficult to keep a child mentally stable in this environment,” Odai’s father told MEE.

“Mobile phones and the stories they hear from friends leave a severe psychological impact on children, especially when they see photos of killed children. That is out of our control.”

He added that such horrifying scenes impact even adults like himself, not just children. He believes the best solution is for local authorities and organisations to provide immediate psychological support during these difficult times.

“During wartime, everyone worries about the physical safety of their children, and only a few care about their psychological well-being - which is just as important, as its long-term impact can be devastating,” he said.

Gap between needs and support

The Taiz Human Rights Centre's Aqlan told MEE: “There are more than 100,000 children in Taiz governorate who have witnessed the horrors of war and been traumatised by its shells, explosions and tragedies. They are in urgent need of psychological care.”

He identified the group most in need of psychological support as the families who have lost loved ones, had their homes shelled, been displaced or have directly suffered from the consequences of the war. 

  
  
      



    Women and children gather at a temporary shelter for displaced people at Shawkani school, north of Aden, Yemen, 15 September 2026 (AFP)
  




  
    



  









In mid-September, prior to the recent escalation around Taiz city, the UN children's agency Unicef reported that over 57,000 children had been displaced in just a two-week period.

While the Taiz Human Rights Centre estimates that over 100,000 children need psychological support in the governorate, the UN reported earlier this year, before the recent military escalation, that 12.2 million children across the country were in need of humanitarian assistance.

The Social Affairs and Labour Office in Taiz governorate stated on Sunday that non-governmental humanitarian organisations operating in the governorate provided psychosocial support services to 719 children, while 219 boys and girls received psychological first aid sessions.

Future at risk  

Psychologist Saba al-Sabri, who works with several institutions providing psychological support in Taiz, confirmed that clear behavioural changes in children have been observed over the past month.

“These behaviours include non-acceptance of others, grief over loss, continuous fear, nervousness, bedwetting, clinging to parents even during sleep, and a total loss of motivation to learn because they believe they will die or become disabled, all of which severely affect the children’s future,” Sabri told MEE. 


  

  Yemen: Parents in Taiz demand answers over alleged rape of their children
    Read More »


She said that the counselling sessions provided by humanitarian initiatives and organisations remain far too few compared to the immense need that has persisted for over 11 years.

“These recent events have added new children to the list of those in need, making psychological support vital to preserving the next generation.”

Sabri pointed out that some parents do not realise the severity of psychological trauma on children, and instead focus solely on basic survival, which represents a disaster for the child.

“Ignoring a child’s feelings and failing to sit and communicate with them leaves a deep negative impact on their well-being.”

Most children currently do not leave their homes. Sabri noted that children are naturally energetic and need to play outside; depriving them of this heightens stress and nervousness, weakens their personality development and worsens their mood.

Abdulellah, the mother of the three children who witnessed the fighting and were traumatised, strongly believes in psychological treatment, but it remains inaccessible to them.

“If psychological treatment were available, I wouldn’t hesitate to take my children. But we are in a time of war, and it is hard to access such services since they are usually only available in the city.”

articles.description:
'Show courage' and end Netanyahu's government, Tibi urges Israeli opposition leader

    
    

        
    
                Speaking to David Hearst, Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi urged Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to show political courage and work with Arab parties to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rule.

"I hope Eisenkot will be courageous enough to go forward and form a minority government, which will end this government of Netanyahu immediately," Tibi said.

In the latest episode of the David Hearst Podcast, Ahmad Tibi, founder and leader of the Ta’al party, said there was no democratic justification for ruling out cooperation with Palestinian representatives in the Knesset this time around.    

Tibi’s party is part of the Joint List, alongside two other Palestinian-led parties, Hadash and Balad. Together, they won 11 seats. Another Palestinian party, Ra’am, secured eight, giving the two slates a combined 19 seats - a record for Palestinian parties in parliament.  

The results mean that neither a Netanyahu-led nor an Eisenkot-led bloc can secure a 61-seat majority without Palestinian parties.

articles.title: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
articles.description:
Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families

    
    

        
    
                After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.

Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.

The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.

For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life.

“Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. I have seven sons and six daughters, yet Fatima was more precious to me than all of them,” Abo Amra told Middle East Eye.

articles.title: Israeli forces kill 19 Palestinians in three days of Gaza attacks
articles.description:
Israeli forces kill 19 Palestinians in three days of Gaza attacks

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 11:29

        
      
    
      
    
                Latest attacks include air strikes on a university and police and security personnel in Khan Younis
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Palestinians inspect the site of an Israeli strike after a vehicle was hit in Gaza City, 2 November 2026 (Reuters/Dawoud Abu Alkas)
                  Off
                  Israeli forces have killed 19 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip since Saturday, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

The ministry said on Tuesday afternoon that six people had been killed in the previous 24 hours, following 13 deaths over the weekend.

One Palestinian succumbed to his wounds on Tuesday morning after Israeli forces bombed the displacement camp where he was staying in Khan Younis.

Another was killed in an air strike targeting a group of people at the University College of Applied Sciences (UCAS) in Khan Younis.

Israeli attacks on school pupils and university students across the Gaza Strip have increased in recent weeks, following the start of the new academic year.
  
    



  



At least 14 pupils and four teachers were killed in Gaza in October, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education.

Three employees of the Islamic University were also killed in an Israeli bombing on campus last month.

The ministry further reported that more than 97 percent of schools and universities in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed by Israeli attacks.

The remaining educational institutions and alternative learning facilities continue to face the threat of further attacks and damage, it added. 

Elsewhere, Gaza's Ministry of Interior reported an Israeli air strike targeting police officers and security personnel in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis.

Several people were killed and wounded, the ministry said, without providing a final death toll. 

Violations of ceasefire

The attacks come as Israel continues to violate the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza.
  
    



  



The US-mediated agreement was intended to halt Israel's genocide by ending the bombardment and lifting restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid.


  

  Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
    Read More »


However, Israel has continued to carry out near-daily air strikes and demolitions of homes.

According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, Israeli forces have killed nearly 1,600 Palestinians since the ceasefire came into effect, including more than 340 children.

A further 5,700 people have been wounded.

The overall Palestinian death toll since the genocide began in October 2023 has reached at least 74,600, according to the ministry. Thousands more people remain missing or buried under the rubble.

Israeli authorities have also continued to impose tight restrictions on the entry of aid and goods into Gaza.

An average of just 200 trucks have been allowed into the territory each day, well below the agreed 600 and the estimated minimum required to meet Gaza's needs.

According to Gaza's Government Media Office, Israeli forces have committed 5,989 violations of the ceasefire since it took effect on 11 October 2025.

These include air strikes, shootings, home demolitions, raids and arbitrary arrests.

articles.title: Israel’s election shows its democracy is a sham, but the West can’t stop buying the lie
How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
articles.description:
How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Lubna Masarwa
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 14:39

        
      
    
      
    
                In Israel today, it doesn't really matter what your politics are. The fact that you are an Arab is proof enough of your guilt
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Right-wing demonstrators gather in support of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who failed to secure a majority in Israeli elections, in Tel Aviv on 31 October 2026 (Jack Guez/AFP)
                  Off
                  A day before the Israeli elections, I was walking through a well-heeled, leafy neighbourhood in West Jerusalem, five minutes from President Issac Herzog’s official residence.

I was on my way to interview an expert on Palestinian citizens of Israel, who were expected to vote in large numbers for the first time.

Three children - they could not have been more than seven or eight - jumped off the slides in a playground and ran towards me. 

One of them asked whom I was going to vote for. A funny question, I thought, coming from kids.  

I told them I would vote for the Joint List. The leader of the group asked, “What is the Joint List? Is it Bibi?” I said no, without explaining that it was an Arab bloc of parties. 
  
    



  



The kid said: “So you’re not voting for Netanyahu?”

I said no. He spat at me, and the other two gave me the middle finger. 

They must have thought I was a Jew defecting from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp. I wondered what they would have done if they knew I was Palestinian.

Kids spitting at a middle-aged woman didn’t seem to bother any of the passersby.

To liberal Zionists, this election was a debate about the boundaries of Israeli democracy, and whether it could include us as Arabs.


Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians


But the more I think about it, something far deeper is going on than mere hatred of a minority group, deeply entrenched though that is. The reaction to 7 October merely brought it out into the open.

Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians, and calling openly for more occupation, expulsion and deportation.

Palestinians who live in the city have to hold their breath if they want to live with this reality. They have no right to complain against another sticker calling on them to be killed or expelled.

It’s not just in every debate in this election campaign. You can hear it in small conversations in the street: “We will not sit with the Arabs.”

All the discussion is about how to build coalitions without the votes of the Arabs. 

Palestinians vote for survival

Three Israeli political parties ran on platforms that openly support the deportation, displacement and expulsion of Palestinians - even those with Israeli citizenship.

Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and head of the Religious Zionism party, has made “Judaising” the Galilee and Negev regions of Israel, where many Palestinians citizens live, a key feature of his election campaign.

All of this was orchestrated by the person who by rights should be Israel’s outgoing prime minister, Netanyahu, but who continues as its caretaker.
  
    



  



Haaretz analysed Netanyahu’s social media activity on election day. Every second post by the prime minister was against Arabs, laying the groundwork for claims about the integrity of the vote.



The response of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up a fifth of the population, was immediate. They flocked to the polls, gaining an unheard-of 19 seats, and became the third-largest parliamentary bloc after Likud and Yashar.

Those who had boycotted elections for their entire lives went to vote for the first time.

This was not some sudden revelation. Every Palestinian understood that they were only part of Israel as window dressing, to make it look democratic, but with no meaningful ability to change their lives. In the past, just over half of them voted.


The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself


But this time, it was different.

The Palestinians of Israel know that what happened in Gaza, and is continuing to happen in the occupied West Bank, could happen to them too.

Israel committed genocide and got away with it. This vote is a survival vote; an expressed, very existential fear. 

Palestinian sociologist Ameer Fakhoury told Middle East Eye: “The moment your existence becomes the central concern, the very meaning of citizenship changes. A citizen, in the substantive sense, should not have to engage in politics simply to avoid death.

“This is not how citizenship is supposed to function. When survival becomes the dominant motivation, the boundaries of ordinary political participation collapse. The symbolic and substantive meaning of citizenship is fundamentally undermined.”

Such a result in a “normal” democratic country would have ended with the opposition winning.

But not in Israel. Netanyahu’s initial loss became an orgy, a festival of racism against Palestinians.

No good or bad Arabs

Channel 12 News reported that on election day and its aftermath, there was a 400 percent rise in racist discourse against Arabs on social media, as Arabs were accused of stealing the elections.

Ayala Hasson, the veteran journalist of Israel’s public broadcaster, Kan 11, claimed, without any proof, that some of the 19 newly elected Knesset members from the Palestinian-led parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, “transferred money to Hamas”.

Hasson, a pro-Netanyahu journalist, also questioned the integrity of the elections, saying that Palestinian voters received envelopes with money as part of an illegal voter mobilisation campaign.

It doesn’t really matter what your politics are. The fact that you are an Arab is proof enough of your guilt.


  

  I have boycotted Israeli elections for years, but this time I will vote
    Read More »


Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has openly adopted a Zionist agenda by acknowledging the Jewish state and calling for national service.

He received the same treatment. This means that even Palestinians who strip themselves of their national identity cannot be part of a political system designed for Jews only.

The same thing happened to Lucy Aharish, an Arab journalist married to an Israeli Jew who served as a combat soldier in the reserves during the genocide in Gaza.

Aharish was savaged by prominent figures in Likud.

Itzik Bonzel, a Likud candidate, posted on Facebook: “You can walk around our streets as much as you like, but merely living among us does not make you Israeli in any way, and you will never be part of us, nor part of the people of Israel.”

Aharish is an opponent of the Palestinian national cause. Bonzel said she was “a foreign body, without any real roots in this land, and you will never be an Israeli”, concluding with a threat: “Know your place.”

Arabs in Israel can no longer ignore the fact that for large groups in Israel, possibly now the majority, there are no good or bad Arabs. It matters not who goes over to their side.
  
    



  



For them, Palestinians are illegitimate and should be expelled from the Jewish state.

The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself - and this should not be ignored by the Palestinian leadership.

I was asked in an interview with a Canadian radio station whether I thought Palestinians would vote again in future elections. Did this result inspire them?

For a moment I was taken aback by the stupidity of this question.

“I am not inspired, I am terrified,” I replied.

                Hassan Salameh was beaten and shot inside his cell, possibly with rubber-coated bullets, after Ben-Gvir stormed the prison, his fiancee and a prisoner rights group say
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A Palestinian boy holds a framed image of Hassan Salameh during a protest against the Israeli death penalty law for Palestinians in Gaza City 31 March (Reuters/Dawoud Abu Alkas)
                  Off
                  Israeli prison guards shot and wounded prominent Palestinian detainee Hassan Salameh nine times last month, his fiancee and a prisoners' rights group have said.

The assault on Salameh, 55, came after National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir stormed his cell and filmed himself threatening to kill him.

The Palestinian Prisoners’ Society (PPS), which monitors the conditions of Palestinian detainees, said it received information about the assault following a visit to Salameh by a lawyer on Monday.

Information provided to the group and Salameh’s fiancee, Ghufran Zamel, indicated that he had been severely beaten and shot nine times.

The type of ammunition used and the precise circumstances of the shooting remain unclear.
  
    



  



Israeli prison guards have recently stepped up the use of rubber-coated bullets against prisoners, firing at them from close range inside their cells.

The practice has caused severe injuries and potentially irreversible harm, according to rights groups. 

PPS said Israeli restrictions on prison visits had prevented the lawyer from obtaining further details.

“This has raised serious concerns about the prisoner's fate and underscores the urgent need to disclose the circumstances of the incident and guarantee his physical safety,” the group said.



Zamel told local media that Salameh was beaten before Ben Gvir's visit and after he left. An Israeli force stormed the cell, subjecting him to a severe beating, including blows to the face, before firing nine bullets at him.

Three days after the assault, Salameh was taken to have his injuries photographed. He was then returned to his cell without medical treatment and given only painkillers, despite the injuries he had sustained, Zamel said.

According to Zamel, Monday's visit by the lawyer confirmed that Salameh was still suffering from the effects of the assault and remained in poor health. He appeared visibly exhausted.

PPS said the attack came amid what it described as a campaign targeting prominent Palestinian prisoners, which goes “beyond repression and punishment” and places their lives at risk.

“Prisoner leaders are facing various forms of physical and psychological torture, systematic crackdowns and public threats to kill them made by Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir,” the group said.

“The continuation of these policies, alongside restrictions on visits and the absence of independent oversight, paves the way for further violations and deprives prisoners of even the most basic protection.”

Escalating abuse 

Born in the Khan Younis refugee camp in southern Gaza in 1971, Salameh became involved in Palestinian resistance against the Israeli occupation after the outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987.

He later became a leading figure in the armed wing of Hamas, the al-Qassam Brigades. In 1996, Israel convicted him of orchestrating several bombings that killed and wounded scores of Israelis.
  
    



  



Salameh said the attacks were carried out in response to Israel's assassination of Hamas bombmaker Yahya Ayyash earlier that year. 


  

  Israeli guards ‘crushed’ Palestinian prisoner’s testicle with rubber bullet
    Read More »


He was sentenced to 48 life terms and has spent a total of 14 years in solitary confinement since his imprisonment 30 years ago.

In September, Ben Gvir posted a video showing himself in Salameh’s cell, surrounded by security guards, as he told him that he wanted to "execute" him.

The minister also vowed to ensure prisoners such as Salameh were "put to death" if he became defence minister.

Palestinian prisoners, particularly prominent figures such as Salameh, have long faced abuse by Israeli prison authorities.

However, reports of abuse have escalated since the Gaza war and genocide began in October 2023. Several rights groups have accused Israeli prison authorities of widespread torture, physical assaults, sexual violence, starvation, medical neglect and humiliation of prisoners since then. 

Last month, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel said they had collected 21 testimonies documenting what they described as a “dangerous practice” of prison guards firing rubber-coated bullets at prisoners from close range.

In one incident, an Israeli prison guard seriously wounded a Palestinian prisoner by firing rubber-coated bullets at his testicle. His right testicle was “completely crushed” and had to be surgically removed.

Israeli ex-generals condemn settler violence, help Palestinian farmers

    
    

        
    
                A group of senior Israeli ex-military officials helped Palestinian farmers on Tuesday to harvest olives, in a gesture of solidarity amid an upsurge in extremist settler violence targeting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

"When I see what is going on here, when I see these guys come... and hit women and kids, it reminds me of stories from my parents from the time when the Jewish people suffered," said former Major General Eyal Ben-Reuven, who compared the settler attacks to pogroms.

Ben-Reuven said he began organising a group of around 30 senior military officials - including six generals - several months ago, following an increase in settler violence that many Palestinians say is enabled by the Israeli military.

"Occupation is the main problem of Israeli society. I believe we must deal with it. We cannot ignore it. We must try to solve it together with the Palestinians," said former Colonel Doron Meinert.

Reporting by Reuters

articles.description:
Opposition leader Lapid accuses Netanyahu backers of attempts at 'crushing' Israel's democracy

    
    

        
    
                Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid has accused supporters of Benajmin Netanyahu's government of attempting to "crush" Tel Aviv's democracy.

"What we are seeing tonight is an attempt to crush democracy and steal the election with the help of government plants in the security system," he said in a post on X.

"This is a direct threat to our democracy from people who are unwilling to admit defeat," Lapid added.

The Israeli opposition leaders also called on state institution to "stand firm" against the move, calling on his counterparts to "put everything aside and form a government as quickly as possible".

Lapid's remarks come amid reports of Shin Bet chief David Zini seeking to question three Palestinian party leaders in an investigation into possible foreign interference in the election.

Netanyahu’s camp has been repeatedly accused in recent days of seeking to delegitimise the election results after claims that the vote for Palestinian-led parties, who won a historic 19 seats out of 120, were manipulated by foreign interference.

Law enforcement officials have found no evidence of such claims or a justification to question the leaders.

The mass participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s election last week obstructed both Netanyahu and his challenger Gadi Eisenkott from gaining the 61 seats required to secure a parliamentary majority and form a government.

articles.title: Shot in class: Gaza's children return to school under Israeli fire
articles.description:
Shot in class: Gaza's children return to school under Israeli fire

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Maha Hussaini
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:19

        
      
    
      
    
                In Gaza’s first formal school year since the genocide, Israeli forces intensify shootings targeting teachers and pupils, alongside air strikes on universities
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Palestinian children walk to school past the rubble of destroyed buildings as the academic year begins in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, 19 September 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP)
                  Off
                  Palestinian teacher Sahar Abushbeika was explaining a science lesson to her third-grade pupils when an Israeli bullet struck her lower back, leaving her bleeding in front of her students.

Within seconds, she collapsed as the children gathered around her, screaming for help.

Abushbeika, who teaches at Dawn of Hope, a makeshift tent school in eastern Khan Younis, southern Gaza, says she was shot by Israeli forces on 30 September.

“It was a normal day. Nothing unusual was happening near the school. I arrived in the morning as usual and began explaining the lesson when I suddenly heard what sounded like a drone, followed by a small explosion,” Abushbeika told Middle East Eye.

“I felt something hit my lower back and realised it was a bullet. The pupils panicked, and I tried to calm them down, but they saw the blood, and I fell to the ground. All I remember is the screams of my students before I found myself in hospital.”
  
    



  



After nearly three years of Israeli attacks that have devastated Gaza’s education system and destroyed or damaged more than 97 percent of schools across the Strip, the Ministry of Education, Unrwa and several independent initiatives have established makeshift tent schools to educate hundreds of thousands of school-age children.

But with classrooms and teachers in short supply, schools have introduced rotating shifts. Many pupils receive only about three hours of lessons a day, three days a week.


'The bullet came close to his heart'

- Muna Abusneimah, Palestinian mother 


Determined to support Gaza’s battered education system and help children make up for years of lost schooling, Abushbeika volunteered to teach at a school near the tent where she now lives, having been displaced from her home in Khan Younis.

“There are no tables or chairs in the school. Pupils sit on the ground, and I stand to explain the lessons. The bullet penetrated the tent and hit me directly,” she said.

Although she was hospitalised, doctors could not remove the bullet because it was lodged in a highly sensitive area of her back. She now has to live with it, unable to walk or even sit properly.

The mother of five says doctors could not prioritise her for medical evacuation, with thousands of patients deemed more urgent already waiting on lengthy evacuation lists.

‘He was in class’

About three weeks later, another pupil was struck by Israeli fire in eastern Khan Younis.

Nine-year-old Amir Abusneimah was sitting with his classmates in a school run by the US-registered charity, the Gaza Children Village, when a bullet pierced the tent classroom, struck the blackboard and ricocheted into his shoulder.

“He was in class when the bullet came from above, passed close to the teacher’s head, hit the board and then ricocheted into his left shoulder. That reduced the severity of his injury,” his mother, Muna Abusneimah, told MEE from her tent in Khan Younis.


  

  Gaza students return to makeshift schools after three years of genocide 
    Read More »


“The bullet came close to his heart. The school called me and said Amir had been wounded in his arm. I ran there and found that they had given him first aid. When he saw me, he tried to reassure me, saying: ‘Don’t worry, Mum, I’m fine. God was kind to me.’” 

Abusneimah said her son was wounded despite sand barriers built around the school tents to protect pupils and staff from Israeli bullets and gunfire, which have become frequent in the displacement camp. The school lies about two to three kilometres from Israel’s so-called Yellow Line.

Just days after he was wounded, MEE was told that an Israeli bullet pierced the school administration room and struck a cupboard while the headteacher was inside.

At Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, doctors determined that Amir needed urgent surgery after discovering that one of his arteries had been severed.

“The surgery lasted about four hours. His condition is now stable, but he still needs physiotherapy,” his mother said.

“He has now stopped going to school because of his injury, but will return when he has recovered.”

Abusneimah, who is raising her five children alone while separated from her husband, says she remains anxious whenever they leave for school.

Attacks on school 

This school year, education began returning across Gaza to something approaching normal for the first time since the genocide began in October 2023. 

But in less than two months since classes resumed, several Israeli attacks on schools and universities have disrupted learning again. 


    Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
    Read More »


In the latest attack, an Israeli air strike hit the entrance to the University College of Applied Sciences in Mawasi Khan Younis on Tuesday, killing three Palestinians and wounding 11 others, including students.

On the same day, student Rimas Ismail al-Madhoun, 16, was killed in an Israeli air strike shortly after she returned from school in the middle of Gaza City. 

On 25 October, two air strikes hit the courtyard of the Islamic University in Gaza City, killing three security guards and wounding several others, including students.

“There is constant gunfire, and people are frequently injured in our displacement camp. I can be sitting in my tent and still feel unsafe,” Abusneimah said.

“I’m always worried when Amir and my other children go to school.”

In October alone, at least 14 school students aged six to 16 were killed in Israeli attacks. Four teachers and three university employees were also killed during the month.

Since 7 October 2023, at least 19,200 school students and 1,386 university students have been killed, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education. 

A further 28,590 school students and 3,100 university students have been wounded.
