articles.title: UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools
articles.description:
UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Oscar Rickett
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:30

        
      
    
      
    
                The Good Law Project and British Jewish group Na'amod tell MEE contested IHRA definition protects Israel, not Jewish students
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Police officers intervene as a pro-Israel banner is held during a rally in London on 16 November 2024 (AFP)
                  Off
                  The British government is being challenged legally over its recommendation for schools to adopt the contested IHRA definition of antisemitism.

The Good Law Project launched a legal challenge against the government on Monday. The group’s executive director Jo Maugham told Middle East Eye he was worried that “rules which conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism… could be among the drivers of antisemitism”. 

“Antisemitism and the rise of antisemitism in Britain and around the world are very real things, and I want to say to British Jews who are at the sharp end, I hear your pain,” Maugham said.

“But I also worry - and it's a point I've made many times - that rules which conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and that unjustifiably constrain the freedom properly and vigorously to criticise Israel, could be amongst the drivers of antisemitism.”

The UK Department of Education’s move to encourage schools to adopt the IHRA definition follows the recommendation made in British education official and academic David Bell's recently published report on antisemitism in the country's schools and colleges.
  
    



  



The Bell report has been questioned for misrepresenting its findings, equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and surveying small numbers of students from a narrow age bracket.

The controversy surrounding the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, which was originally formulated in 2004 as a non-legally binding tool to assist in monitoring antisemitism, comes mainly from the fact that seven of its 11 “illustrations” of antisemitism include references to Israel.


'Jewish pupils should be safe at school, and antisemitism has to be taken seriously. The IHRA definition doesn’t do that job'

- Na'amod


The definition’s lead author, Kenneth Stern, has warned against its use as a disciplinary or legal instrument, arguing that it may risk restricting legitimate political expression.

In 2018, leading human rights lawyer Geoffrey Robertson issued a legal opinion stating that the definition is “likely in practice to chill free speech” by encouraging complaints against legitimate criticism of Israel.

The British Jewish group Na’amod, which also opposes the imposition of the IHRA definition, told MEE: “Jewish pupils should be safe at school, and antisemitism has to be taken seriously. The IHRA definition doesn’t do that job.”

“Its examples run criticism of Israel together with hatred of Jews, and in universities it has overwhelmingly been used to censor speech about Israel rather than to protect Jews,” a spokesperson for the group added.

“In schools, that leaves teachers policing children who talk about Gaza or the Nakba, instead of tackling real anti-Jewish racism. It also fails Jewish pupils, many of whom don’t tie their Jewishness to support for the Israeli state.”

The Bell review

The IHRA definition has been formally adopted by 47 countries.

Its adoption in British schools was one of 27 recommendations made in the Bell review. Following its publication on 21 October, it was widely reported that “three in five” Jewish students had experienced antisemitism in English schools.

This figure came from a survey of 5,000 students, 92 of whom were Jews aged, between 16 and 18. Seventy of those students responded to a question about whether they had personally experienced or witnessed antisemitism, with 29 of them - 41 percent, or around “two in five” rather than “three in five” - saying they had.


  

  UK antisemitism report found increase in 'anti-Israel' sentiment, not 'anti-Jewish' attitudes
    Read More »


The Bell review itself acknowledged that this was a “low sample size” and should be “treated with caution”. It also found that “anti-Jewish attitudes are typically less prevalent and have remained more stable, whereas anti-Israel sentiments are more prevalent and have been increasing”.

Middle East Eye asked the UK Department for Education about its plans to adopt the IHRA definition and about whether it had considered the warnings - including from the definition’s lead author - about the “chilling effect” the definition can have on pro-Palestinian expression and criticism of Israel.

“Antisemitism is a growing problem across society, including in our schools and colleges, and Jewish children and staff should never face hatred or prejudice in education,” a Department for Education spokesperson said in response.

“That is why we have accepted all 27 of Sir David Bell’s recommendations and are acting on them, including encouraging schools and colleges to adopt the IHRA working definition of antisemitism.

“The IHRA definition has been adopted by 47 countries and countless public bodies and can provide a practical framework for teachers and pupils, and help give greater clarity on how to identify and tackle antisemitism wherever it occurs.”

'Consistency is what we want'

Bell’s review recommends separate measures for tackling anti-Jewish hatred, distinct from existing anti-racism and anti-bullying policies. The National Education Union has criticised the move, warning it risks “creating a hierarchy of racism”.

The Good Law Project and Na’amod both told MEE that the British government should be consistent in how it deals with racism and not apply special treatment to antisemitism.


'It is not merely important to protect the space to advance vigorous criticisms of Israel’s appalling actions. We think it is necessary in a moral society'

- Jo Maugham, Good Law Project


“What we really want is for government to be consistent in how it tackles hate speech,” Maugham said. 

“The rules that apply to one minoritised group should also be the rules that are applied to other minoritised groups… Consistency is what we want.”

“Antisemitism should not be taught as exceptional,” the spokesperson for Na’amod said. “It should be taught alongside racism and Islamophobia, because these struggles are bound together and the people who fight one are the natural allies of those who fight the others.

“Treating antisemitism as a special case with its own rulebook prevents that learning and sets Jewish safety apart from everyone else’s.”

Gary Spedding, a cross-party political consultant on Israel-Palestine, told MEE he thought Bell’s review was “sloppy, misleading and inaccurate”, and that it was part of a “systemic, legal and institutional dismantling of any support for Palestine, or any education and discussion about Palestinian history and existence within the UK education system”.

Pro-Israel influence in British schools

Over the past decade, the Department for Education and British government ministers have issued warnings to headteachers, teaching staff and local authorities over how Palestine is approached in schools.

These interventions have often come after lobbying from pro-Israel groups such as UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI), the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Community Security Trust (CST).


'Palestine is viewed as a partisan issue triggering school neutrality, but Zionism and Israel are not'

- Gary Spedding, political consultant on Israel-Palestine


In 2021, the BBC removed a seven-part series of educational videos about Palestine from its GCSE Bitesize platform - a free classroom resource for teachers - following pressure from UKLFI. 

Former Conservative education secretaries Gavin Williamson and Gillian Keegan both formally instructed headteachers to ensure “political impartiality” when it came to discussions on Israel-Palestine in schools. 

“Palestine is viewed as a partisan issue triggering school neutrality, but Zionism and Israel are not,” Spedding told MEE. “Meanwhile, the activities of pro-Israel advocacy organisations, operating in and having access to UK schools, do not receive an equivalent level of UK government or institutional scrutiny,” he said. 

A plethora of pro-Israel groups, including StandWithUs UK, United Jewish Israel Appeal and JNF UK provide educational resources, speakers and trips to Israel for British students and teachers.

StandWithUs has said that it helps students “stand strong in the face of antisemitism and anti-Zionism”, while the JNF allows them to “explore Israel” and offers “workshops on Zionist history”.

“Israel advocacy organisations try to argue their presence in the school system is necessary to counter rising antisemitism and anti-Zionism in schools,” Spedding said.

“But our educational unions have noted that the resulting imbalance leaves teachers highly anxious about covering topics related to Palestine, answering pupils’ questions and queries with regard to Palestine, and that traditional pro-Israel and Zionist viewpoints go largely unscrutinised by the UK government.”

“It is not merely important to protect the space to advance vigorous criticisms of Israel’s appalling actions,” Maugham reiterated. “We think it is necessary in a moral society.”

US midterm elections 2026: Top Democrat tells Trump administration to 'lawyer up'
articles.description:
US midterm elections 2026: Top Democrat tells Trump administration to 'lawyer up'

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 14:35

        
      
    
      
    
                Robert Garcia has vowed to investigate the Trump family's business dealings. Among the issues under scrutiny could be UAE investments and a deal involving Abu Dhabi-backed investors
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US Congressman Robert Garcia convenes a hearing in West Palm Beach, Florida, 12 May 2026 (Joe Raedle/Getty Images via AFP)
                  Off
                  A senior Democrat has warned US President Donald Trump and his Republican allies to "lawyer up", vowing to investigate alleged corruption and the business dealings of the president's family following the party's midterm election victories.

Speaking to Punchbowl News on Tuesday, Robert Garcia, who is expected to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, said Democrats would use their congressional powers to scrutinise the Trump family's financial interests.

The California Democrat said he would investigate "Trump crypto schemes" and how members of the president's family, including Jared Kushner, were "sitting on boards and getting contracts".

"Anyone who has been in bed with the Trumps" would have "no choice but to respond to our questions", he said.

Hours later, Garcia issued a blunt two-word warning: "Lawyer up."
  
    



  



Garcia has previously pledged to investigate what he called the "Trump Crime Family", as well as corporate corruption, alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the handling of the Epstein files.

Among the issues likely to attract scrutiny are the Trump family's lucrative business relationships with foreign investors and government-linked figures, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.

In January 2025, four days before Trump's inauguration, UAE-backed investors agreed to pay $500m for a 49 percent stake in World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded by Trump's sons, Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump.

The investment was backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE's national security adviser and brother of the country's president.

According to the Wall Street Journal, $187m of the initial payment went to entities linked to the Trump family, while $31m went to companies associated with Steve Witkoff, Trump's Middle East envoy and a co-founder of the venture.

Conflict of interest?

The deal raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, particularly after the Trump administration subsequently approved the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips to the UAE, easing restrictions imposed under former President Joe Biden.

A separate deal involving Abu Dhabi-backed investors also brought World Liberty Financial under scrutiny.
  
    



  



In May 2025, MGX, an investment firm backed by Abu Dhabi, announced a $2bn investment in cryptocurrency exchange Binance, using World Liberty's USD1 stablecoin to facilitate the transaction.

While MGX was the investor and Binance the recipient, the use of USD1 potentially generated interest income and other commercial benefits for World Liberty through the assets backing the stablecoin.

The arrangement attracted further scrutiny after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao was pardoned by Trump in October 2025, after pleading guilty in 2023 to violating US anti-money-laundering requirements.


  

  US midterm elections 2026: Democrats sweep House and Senate in major rebuke to Trump
    Read More »


According to a June 2026 report by Democratic staff on the Senate Banking Committee, at least 10 Trump administration policy actions benefiting the UAE followed investments in Trump family cryptocurrency ventures. 

Trump's family and close associates have also established lucrative financial relationships with Saudi Arabia, raising further questions about potential conflicts of interest.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and former senior White House adviser, secured a $2bn investment from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) for his private equity firm, Affinity Partners, after leaving the first Trump administration.

The fund is chaired by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, widely known as MBS, with whom Kushner developed close ties during his time in the White House.

The Trump Organisation has also pursued property and licensing ventures across the Gulf, including projects in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Oman. These include luxury residential developments, hotels and golf resorts promoted by Trump's sons.

According to the Oversight Democrats' 2026 report, Trump and his family are believed to have generated $2.25bn in realised profits from digital currency ventures and other foreign-linked payments. The figure rises to as much as $9.72bn when estimated unrealised wealth is included.

Speaking ahead of Tuesday's election, Trump indicated that he would consider issuing pre-emptive pardons to himself and his aides if they faced investigations led by Democrats.

"I would if needed to," he told The Post's Pod Force One host Miranda Devine.

"I would not even think about it. I'd do it."

articles.title: Inspired by UK sanctions on Israel, US Democrats want to work with Labour
articles.description:
Inspired by UK sanctions on Israel, US Democrats want to work with Labour

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Peter Oborne
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 12:47

        
      
    
      
    
                A source told MEE that informal talks are already taking place between Democrats and the Burnham government
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband attends a panel discussion during the Warsaw Security Forum in Warsaw, Poland on 13 October (AFP)
                  Off
                  As US President Donald Trump reels from Tuesday night’s election wipeout, victorious Democrats are praising British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for inspiring new US policies towards Israel.

Democrats have told MEE that they plan to take advantage of their new hold over Congress to introduce sanctions aimed at settlers in the occupied West Bank, which would be in line with British sanctions introduced last month.

There is also talk on both sides of the Atlantic of reviving the traditional alliance between Labour and Democrats as the 2028 presidential election approaches. 

One source told MEE that informal talks are already taking place between Democrats and the Burnham government amidst expectations of a “strong relationship between a progressive Democratic president and a progressive UK prime minister”.

Democrat sources told MEE they watched British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Miliband break with Keir Starmer’s foreign policy towards Israel - and noted how popular it has been in Britain.
  
    



  



Even before last night’s momentous results, some Democrats have been publicly calling for the US to copy Labour’'s sanctions policy.

Texas Congressman Joaquin Castro described Miliband’s sanctions announcement as “a step in the right direction”. 


  

  Exclusive: Miliband set on sanctions regardless of Israel election outcome as officials try to weaken measures
    Read More »


He denounced settlement expansion as a “land grab carried out through violence and terrorism” before calling on the US to follow Britain’s lead.

Congressman Ro Khanna, who was held at gunpoint by settlers in the West Bank last summer, praised the UK’s “important moral step”. 

Matt Duss, a Washington Middle East expert with strong links to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, told MEE on Tuesday night that “seeing key allies taking these steps gives a real boost to colleagues in the US”. 

He added that, “A new class of progressive Democrat is coming into Congress who wants to support Palestinian rights.”

Democratic member of Congress, Greg Casar, has already urged a US ban on trade with the settlements.

Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, meanwhile, declared that “Congress can and must act”.

'It is time' 

Emily Thornberry, the chair of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Select Committee, told MEE that if "brave and thoughtful leaders such as Reps Khanna, Casar and Castro are put into a position to develop US policy toward Israel and the occupied territories, real progress could be made."

Thornberry added: “I would recommend what we have done [on Israeli settlements] as a model, and I dearly hope that we’re able to work together on this in the near future.”

In a sign that the Democrats have been inspired by Britain, 19 Senate Democrats - including Castro and Casar - introduced legislation in late September to sanction people or companies facilitating settlement construction as part of the Israeli government’s E1 plan.

The plan involves building thousands of new housing units between Jerusalem and the existing West Bank settlement of Maale Adumim, 7km east of the city. It would effectively cut the West Bank in half, making a Palestinian state unviable.

Congresswoman Madeleine Dean, one of the lawmakers behind the sanctions bill, said when it was unveiled: “It is time that the United States joined our allies - such as the United Kingdom, France, and Canada - in taking action to help preserve dignity and self-determination for the Palestinian people, which is essential for progress toward peace.”
  
    



  



Both the Sunak and Starmer governments pursued a general policy of alignment with the US. Then came Burnham’s startling break with the Trump administration over Israel, with Britain leading middle-ranking powers including France and Canada in sanctioning settlements in September.

This bold move opened up a new interest in Britain from the US Democrats, who have emerged victorious in the American midterms this week.


'I dearly hope that we’re able to work together on this [policy towards Israel] in the near future'

 - Emily Thornberry, Foreign Affairs Select Committee chair


Polls have shown most of the British public, including a narrow majority of Conservative voters, supported the sanctions package.

Democrats are hoping to distance themselves from former US President Joe Biden’s support for Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza. 

With high-profile Democratic candidates critical of Israel - in particular Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who was relentlessly attacked by Trump but endorsed by former Democratic President Barack Obama - storming to victory in the midterms this week, the appetite within the Democratic Party to take a tougher stance on Israel is nearly certain to increase.

This may especially be so if Trump now launches a fresh assault with Israel on Iran - which the midterm results indicate most Americans do not support. 

In some ways, the burgeoning alliance between the Democrats and Labour recalls the close ties built up between US President Bill Clinton and Tony Blair before he became prime minister in 1997.

The relationship between Harold Wilson and Lyndon Johnson in the 1960s is another example.

A close relationship between the Democrats and Labour would therefore mark a return to traditional British foreign policy, which has been strongly tied to the United States.

articles.title: Israeli army ends 11-day Hebron raid after looting and vandalising Palestinian homes
articles.description:
Israeli army ends 11-day Hebron raid after looting and vandalising Palestinian homes

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Fayha Shalash
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 14:24

        
      
    
      
    
                Residents return to damaged houses stripped of valuables as military assault leaves hundreds displaced, businesses destroyed and West Bank city facing millions of dollars in losses
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A Palestinian man looks on as he assess the damage to his home after the Israeli military ended an assault in Hebron in theoccupied West Bank, 2 November 2026 (Reuters/Mussa Qawasma)
                  Off
                  For 11 days, Abbas Mujahid imagined returning home. He had no idea when that might be.

Israeli soldiers had forced him and his family of seven to leave the house in Hebron in the occupied West Bank last month. 

Their home is in the al-Jalda neighbourhood of Hebron, the focus of an Israeli military assault that began on 23 October and ended on Monday.

During the attack, hundreds of Palestinian families were displaced by Israeli forces. Major roads and streets were closed, the city’s entrances sealed, and a total blockade imposed. Commercial shops were raided, while industrial facilities were vandalised or demolished.

The assault caused extensive damage to residential neighbourhoods, businesses and infrastructure. Hebron now faces the daunting task of assessing the destruction, clearing debris and reviving an economy brought to a standstill by the blockade.
  
    



  



When Mujahid and his family finally returned, they found their home severely damaged and vandalised.

“We found all the wooden doors, as well as the main iron door, torn off their hinges,” he told Middle East Eye. 

“The gypsum decorative elements were completely smashed, the light fixtures broken, and our clothes and belongings scattered all over the house.” 

According to Mujahid, soldiers had also left human excrement throughout the house. Window frames had been ripped out, apparently in acts of deliberate destruction.


'My only ‘guilt’, the only reason my facility was demolished, is that I am Palestinian'

- Iyad al-Qawasmi, Hebron business owner 


During their displacement, Mujahid had tried to prepare his children for the possibility that their home, particularly their bedrooms, might be badly damaged. But nothing could spare them the shock of seeing the destruction first-hand.

“I have begun bringing in workers to repair the house, its walls, and its doors, at a cost estimated in the tens of thousands of shekels. Yet, the very fact that we have returned outweighs any sense of the damage caused,” he said.

The economic toll has been equally severe. According to estimates by the Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, direct losses exceeded 12 million shekels a day (around $3.8m). A total of 327 commercial and economic establishments were shut down, 15 facilities destroyed and around 1,350 people lost their livelihoods.

The humanitarian impact was also substantial. On 30 October, Unicef reported, citing Hebron Municipality figures, that 483 families had been displaced by Israeli forces and restrictions on the city. They comprised 4,304 people, including 1,845 children.

Heavy losses

The military incursion came after a shooting by two Palestinians that killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron. The two Palestinians were also killed in the fire exchange. 

Israel has been accused of collective punishment with its response, which included mass displacement and demolitions. 

At least 15 homes and facilities were demolished, including three residential properties. Two belonged to the Palestinians who carried out the shooting attack.

Destruction extended beyond demolitions, with private property, household possessions and the contents of commercial establishments also damaged. Business owners and their employees were left facing mounting losses.

Among those affected was Iyad al-Qawasmi, who owned a used vehicle parts business in Farsh al-Hawa, an area where several factories and commercial shops were demolished on 23 October.
  
    



  



Israeli soldiers raided his three-dunum facility, which housed 600 used vehicles, and gave him one hour to evacuate before its demolition.

When Qawasmi asked for a written demolition order, rather than a verbal instruction, soldiers told him an Israeli court had issued the decision and that he had to comply.

  
  
      



    People check the damage after Israeli machinery demolished a Palestinian building near Hebron in the occupied West Bank, 3 November 2026 (Reuters/Mussa Qawasma)
  







He said he had received no prior notice. Since opening the business in 2016, he added, the facility had never been raided, apart from one incident in which surveillance cameras were confiscated.

Qawasmi brought in a bulldozer in an attempt to salvage what he could within the limited time. But several bulldozers belonging to the Israeli army and settlers then entered the site.

They seized at least 400 vehicles, along with other equipment.

“On top of my losses, which exceed 2.5 million shekels ($790,000), they confiscated the vehicles and stole the property I had inside the facility,” he said.
  
    



  



Days later, Israeli bulldozers returned and demolished the facility, reducing it to rubble. The destruction was so complete that the mountains of Halhul, previously obscured by the site, are now visible through it.

Qawasmi remains barred from accessing the land, leaving him unable to retrieve equipment or recover any belongings.

The business employed at least ten people, all of whom supported their families. Its destruction has therefore cut off the income of ten households, affecting at least 70 Palestinians.

“My only ‘guilt’, the only reason my facility was demolished, is that I am Palestinian. The facility is not even located near the site of the shooting incident,” he said.

The road to recovery

Relevant authorities have begun surveying the damage, but rebuilding what was destroyed and restoring normal life will take considerable time and resources.

Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari said the full extent of the damage to private property is still being assessed and documented.


  

  ‘We left with heavy hearts’: Israel’s assault displaces thousands in Hebron
    Read More »


He said the destruction went beyond structural damage. Residents had reported the theft of gold jewellery, cash and personal belongings, as well as broken doors and damaged household contents. 

“A government committee has been formed to assess these damages. Engineers are currently visiting the affected homes to conduct surveys and document the losses, in order to determine the exact scale of the destruction,” he said.

Damage to municipal facilities and utility networks is estimated at around six million shekels (around $1.9m), al-Jabari added.

The losses include damaged streets, pavements, water and electricity lines, as well as municipal equipment, machinery and networks across the city.

During the assault, the municipality managed the emergency through its response committee, staff and equipment. But restoring normal life and repairing the damage will take time.

“Restoring the city to its normal state and repairing the damage it sustained will require at least a month,” he said.

articles.title: Police urged to investigate London event advertising settlement-linked Israeli agency
articles.description:
Police urged to investigate London event advertising settlement-linked Israeli agency

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Imran Mulla
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:23

        
      
    
      
    
                Activists protested at the World Travel Market event, which began on Tuesday and is advertising the Jerusalem Development Authority
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A line of police wait to move in as protesters gather around the corner in support of the Palestine Action activist group outside the Supreme Court in central London on 4 November 2026 (AFP)
                  Off
                  The Metropolitan Police have been urged to investigate the participation of an Israeli agency involved in the construction of illegal settlements at an international travel event in London.

MEE revealed last week that the World Travel Market (WTM) event this week, which faced a pro-Palestine protest on Tuesday and will continue until Thursday, was set to feature a stand run by the Israeli government's tourist office.

The International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP, a UK-based legal group, sent a letter to the Met Police's war crimes team on Tuesday demanding the "urgent investigation and consideration of preventative measures in relation to the reported participation of the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA), through its tourism platform iTravelJerusalem, at World Travel Market (WTM) London".

Activists with the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) protested next to Israel's stand on Tuesday, holding a banner reading "Every settlement is a war crime".

Video footage showed two activists being physically removed from the event by security guards.
  
    



  



Ryvka Barnard, the deputy director of the PSC, told MEE: "The Israeli state's presence at the World Travel Market in London is an utter disgrace. 

"In September, when the foreign secretary acknowledged that Israel's occupation is illegal, he said he would ban the advertising of illegal settlements. But that's exactly what's happening here. 

"This is now a test for the Labour government. Will it stick to its word, intervene to shut down this stall and call for criminal investigations into its organisers, or will it reveal that those were just empty words?"

Will it stick to its word, intervene to shut down this stall and call for criminal investigations into its organisers, or will it reveal that those were just empty words?"

The Israeli stand is shared by numerous Israeli companies and organisations, including "iTravelJerusalem", which promotes tourism in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and is managed by the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA).

The JDA, a statutory agency of the Israeli government and the Jerusalem municipality, carries out development initiatives across Jerusalem and has been heavily involved in the construction and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements on occupied Palestinian territory.

Since 2023 the JDA has a contract with Finn Partners, a global marketing agency, to advertise Jerusalem as a tourism destination in Britain.
  
    



  



'These circumstances warrant urgent investigation'

The ICJP's letter to the Met Police, seen by MEE, says: "Of particular concern is the commercial relationship between the JDA and WTM London... including the possibility that the organisers may receive exhibition fees or derive other financial benefits from the participation of an agency reportedly implicated in settlement related activities.

"We consider that these circumstances warrant urgent investigation into potential offences."

MEE has asked the Met Police and WTM for comment.


  

  Exclusive: London event advertises Israeli agency building illegal settlements
    Read More »


This comes after 15 MPs wrote to the British government on Monday calling for "urgent action" on the event.

The MPs demanded that the government "contact the organisers of WTM London and require the removal of exhibitors and promotional material where their participation would facilitate or promote illegal Israeli settlements".

Last month, the British government recognised Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory as illegal and announced comprehensive sanctions on Israeli settlements.

According to a 2025 report by the Office of the European Union Representative for the West Bank and Gaza Strip, the JDA planned "for the eviction of the Umm Haroun compound - home to approximately 40 Palestinian families - and the construction of a 320-unit settlement" in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood. 

In 2020, a JDA project to build a cable car in Jerusalem, which would involve the uprooting of trees and displacement of infrastructure including water, sewage and telecommunications, was approved by the Israeli government.

The JDA also plans to build a large settlement housing project next to the Palestinian community of Beit Safafa in East Jerusalem.

Hussam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to Britain, said in response to MEE's report last Thursday: "Next week Israeli companies guilty of ethnic cleansing will be platformed at [WTM London]."

Zomlot added: "The UK government must now turn their words into action: enforce these commitments and ensure those complicit in illegal occupation and settlements face real consequences."
